keyVerseText: I will not conceal his parts, nor his power , nor his comely proportion.
rootMeaning: The root of חִין (chîyn) is closely related to חֵן (chên), which conveys the idea of favor, grace, and charm. This root emphasizes not only external beauty but also an inward graciousness or acceptance that is pleasing and precious. Understanding חִין as another form of חֵן enriches its meaning beyond mere physical attractiveness, highlighting a gracious quality that invites favor and delight.
usageInScripture: The word חִין appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Job 41:12, where it is translated as 'comely' or 'comely proportion.' This singular occurrence limits the range of its use but underscores its connection to physical form and grace. The translation as 'nor his comely' suggests a focus on the pleasing or elegant aspect of the creature described, consistent with the root idea of graciousness and favor.
theologicalSignificance: The concept of חִין reminds believers that beauty and grace are not merely superficial but reflect God's creative favor and design. In Scripture, grace encompasses both the inner and outer qualities that make something or someone pleasing to God and others. Recognizing this word's depth encourages a faith perspective that values God's graciousness as foundational to all creation and human dignity. It also points toward the ultimate grace found in Christ, who embodies divine favor and beauty in the fullest sense.
keyVerseReflection: Job 41:12 states, 'I will not conceal his parts, nor his power, nor his comely proportion.' Here, חִין highlights the elegant and gracious design of the creature's form, emphasizing that its beauty is part of its formidable nature. The use of this word in the verse draws attention to God's intentional craftsmanship, reminding us that even fearsome creatures bear the mark of divine favor and purpose.
